where: Lead, Section 1 lead-in and Quiz Q2 answer
problem: The text says the EEG and EMG sources differ by 'about a thousand times', and Q2 repeats that surface EMG is 'about a thousand times larger' than EEG. This contradicts the chapter's own ranges: EEG is 10–100 µV, surface EMG is 0.1–5 mV (100–5000 µV). The real ratio is roughly 10 to 500, typically about 20–50 for a 50 µV EEG against a 1–2 mV EMG, which is why the gains quoted are 10⁴ against 10²–10³ (a factor of 10–100, not 1000). A student will memorise the wrong ratio and then wonder why the gains differ only tenfold.
fix: Say the EMG signal is typically 20–50 times larger (10–500 times across the full ranges), so a lower gain of 10²–10³ is enough. Keep the 1000× point only for the unit conversion: 1 mV = 1000 µV, so check units before choosing gain.

problem: The chain 'band-pass filter, notch filter, rectifier, low-pass smoothing, then root mean square (RMS)' mixes two alternative amplitude measures. RMS already includes the averaging that the low-pass smoothing does, so applying RMS after smoothing adds nothing and confuses the student.
fix: Give two clear alternatives: rectify then low-pass smooth to get the mean absolute (averaged rectified) value; or rectify then compute RMS over a window. Do the RMS on the filtered (or rectified) signal directly, in one step.

where: Section 3, first bullet of the checks paragraph
problem: 'EEG at 50 µV through EMG gain 10³ gives 0.05 V, close to noise' is loose. 50 mV output is well above the amplifier noise floor; the real trouble is that it is only a small part of the 0.5–1 V ADC range, so the digitised trace has poor resolution.
fix: Write: 'EEG at 50 µV through EMG gain 10³ gives only 0.05 V, a small fraction of the ADC range, so resolution is poor and the gain error shows.'

where: Section 1, sampling paragraph and Exam trap 4
problem: The text concludes that a 125 Hz Nyquist frequency makes sampling 'safe', but noise and muscle activity above 125 Hz will still fold back into the 0–70 Hz band unless an anti-aliasing low-pass filter sits before the ADC.
fix: Add one sentence: an anti-aliasing low-pass filter set near 70–100 Hz goes before the ADC, so that content above the Nyquist frequency never reaches the sampler.
